newsitem.title: USA: Former Olympic blast suspect speaks out on Monday.
newsitem.headline: Former Olympic blast suspect speaks out on Monday.

text.p: Three months after being branded a suspect in the fatal Olympic park bombing, Richard Jewell will speak out on Monday about his ordeal and his plans for the future now that the FBI has cleared him.

The 33-year-old former policeman, who went from being a hero to the case's only named suspect in just three days last July, was finally cleared of suspicion on Saturday when the Justice Department issued a letter saying he was no longer a target of the FBI bomb investigation.
Jewell's nationally televised news conference is scheduled for noon EST (1700 GMT) at a hotel in suburban Atlanta.

The letter to his lawyer ended a nightmare of frenzied media attention and round-the-clock FBI surveillance for the security guard suspected of planting a pipe bomb that killed two people and injured more than 100 at the Summer Olympics.

Jewell now has a number of book and movie offers, and his lawyers are expected to sue news organisations, including the Atlanta Journal-Constitution and NBC, for allegedly defaming his character and ruining his chances of finding another job. The first lawsuit is expected to be filed by December 1.
And, despite his public exonertation, they are still considering a lawsuit against the federal government.
"We will carefully examine whether Richard's constitutional rights were violated during the search and the interrogation in July," said lawyer Wayne Grant.

Jewell was working as a security guard at Centennial Olympic Park in downtown Atlanta on July 27 when he spotted a suspicious green knapsack that had been left at a crowded outdoor concert. He alerted police and helped clear people from the area before the bomb inside the sack detonated, sending nails and other shrapnel tearing through the crowd.

Jewell was hailed as a hero for his actions. But on July 30, an article in the Journal-Constitution named him as a focus of the investigation. Within hours, his apartment was besieged by hundreds of journalists who saw federal agents haul away his property in boxes after a mammoth FBI search. A troop of reporters remained at the site for weeks thereafter.
Jewell's exoneration is potentially embarrassing for both the federal criminal justice system and the news media.
The U.S. Attorney's Office has said it would release sealed FBI affidavits this week, detailing the evidence that first led investigators to suspect Jewell planted the bomb.
His lawyers said Jewell had been fingered out only because the FBI felt he matched a profile describing the bomber as a former law enforcement officer with a penchant for heroism.
In a public statement that accompanied his letter, the U.S. attorney admitted that the highly public nature of the Jewell case had actually interfered with the investigation.
This appeared to back up opinions of criminal justice experts who said the focus on Jewell drew FBI manpower and resources away from leads that could have been followed.
Despite reports that the FBI has identified half a dozen potential suspects in its ongoing probe, the investigation to date has shown no sign of closing in on the real bomber.
